items.title: Social and Structural Determinants of Chronic Pain Among Migrant Workers: A Scoping Review Using an Intersectionality Framework
items.abstract: Background: Due to structural inequities, many migrant workers face adverse health outcomes potentially exposing them to long-term pain issues. However, the extent of current knowledge on chronic pain (>3 months) in this population is unclear. As labor migration policies evolve toward less protective measures, it is essential to gain insights into the experiences and drivers of chronic pain among migrant workers. Aims: Drawing on the theoretical framework of intersectionality, this scoping review aimed to synthesize existing knowledge on chronic pain among migrant workers in Canada and the United States. More precisely, we examined evidence related to epidemiology, treatments, lived experiences, and the role of social and structural determinants. Methods: This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews. A search of four databases was followed by a screening and extraction procedure involving four researchers. Relevant findings were reported through quantified and narrative syntheses. Results: This scoping review highlights a major gap in understanding pain chronicity among migrant workers. Nine studies met the eligibility criteria. Most studies have focused on occupational health outcomes. Definitions of chronic pain are inconsistent. Only one qualitative study examined migrant workers' pain trajectories beyond workplace settings. Social and structural determinants were underscored in all studies, including poor working conditions, socioeconomic precarity, unfavorable labor market structure, restrictive immigration policies, racism and discrimination, and gendered inequities. Conclusions: This review invites researchers and policymakers to move beyond occupational health approaches to fully appraise and tackle the intersecting structural and political drivers exposing migrant workers to lifelong experiences of chronic pain.

items.title: Social Networking Usage, Informal Workplace Learning and Personal Professional Development: A Structural Equation Model on the Teachers’ Attitudes and Beliefs towards ICT Adoption in Public Schools
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine the influence of social networking use, informal workplace learning, and personal professional development on teachers' attitudes and beliefs towards ICT adoption among public secondary school teachers in Region XI, Philippines. Standardized survey questionnaires were adopted and contextualized to suit the regional educational setting. The instruments were administered to 417 randomly selected teachers using stratified random sampling. This study employed a quantitative, non-experimental research design, using means, Pearson's r, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) for data analysis. The results revealed generally low to very low levels of social networking usage, informal workplace learning, personal professional development, and attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption. Despite these modest levels, significant positive relationships were found between social networking use and teachers' attitudes toward ICT adoption, as well as between personal professional development and these attitudes. Furthermore, the structural equation modeling results indicated that the three independent variables significantly influenced teachers' attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption, with social networking usage emerging as the strongest predictor among the constructs. The findings underscore the importance of enhancing digital engagement, strengthening informal learning cultures, and providing sustained professional development initiatives to foster more positive attitudes and stronger readiness for ICT integration in schools.

items.title: Socioeconomic determinants of academic motivation in higher education: A systematic review and critical synthesis of international evidence
items.abstract: Academic motivation in higher education constitutes a multidimensional construct shaped by structural conditions that influence students’ academic performance, persistence, and educational trajectories. In contexts characterized by persistent social inequalities, understanding how socioeconomic status (SES) configures motivational processes is essential for the development of university policies aimed at equity and educational sustainability. The purpose of this study was to conduct a critical synthesis of international evidence on the mechanisms through which socioeconomic factors influences academic motivation in higher education during the period period 2017–2020 and 2022–2025. A systematic review was carried out in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and replicability. The literature search was conducted in the Scopus database using structured Boolean search equations. After applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 33 empirical studies were selected for the final analysis. The results of the systematic synthesis reveal sustained growth in scientific output and progressive geographic diversification of the field. Cross-sectional quantitative studies predominate, employing regression models and structural analyses to examine the relationship between parental educational level, financial support, and intrinsic motivation or academic engagement. In addition, several studies incorporate mediating variables such as self-efficacy, institutional integration, and sense of belonging, revealing non-linear explanatory configurations. Overall, the evidence indicates that the influence of socioeconomic status operates through both direct and indirect mechanisms linked to cultural capital and institutional resources. This review identifies key theoretical convergences as well as recurrent methodological limitations within the field. Finally, the findings underscore the need for longitudinal studies and multilevel approaches to deepen the understanding of motivational inequalities in higher education.

items.title: Solid Lipid Nanoparticles and Nanostructured Lipid Carriers in Drug Delivery: A Review
items.abstract: Many pharmacological compounds suffer from poor aqueous solubility, variable bioavailability, fast degradation, unfavorable biodistribution and dose-related side effects, which restrict their therapeutic efficacy. Conventional dosage forms may not achieve the appropriate drug concentrations within the therapeutic window, necessitating the development of improved delivery platforms. Lipid-based nanocarriers, especially solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), provide intriguing methods owing to their biocompatibility, biodegradability and formulation diversity. SLNs are composed of a largely solid lipid matrix supported by surfactants, while NLCs are a mixture of solid and liquid lipids that form a less ordered matrix with more drug accommodation and less drug ejection during storage. This review critically discusses recent advances, with emphasis on literature published during 2021–2026, on the evolution, classification, structural characteristics, formulation components, preparation and characterization, drug-loading and release mechanisms, biological fate, surface engineering, administration routes, and therapeutic applications of SLNs and NLCs. Special attention is paid to safety, regulatory issues, scale-up, commercialization and emerging technologies including artificial intelligence-assisted optimization and microfluidic production. [There has been] considerable preclinical progress but little clinical translation. Long term stability, reproducible large scale manufacturing, regulatory uniformity, and rigorous clinical validation are significant difficulties that need to be systematically investigated.

items.title: SpaceMates: A Tabletop Robotic Tangible Programming System Designed to Cultivate Spatial Reasoning Skills in Middle Childhood
items.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a key cognitive foundation for children’s STEM learning, yet existing tools focus on 2D tasks or programming logic, with limited integration of multidimensional spatial reasoning, embodied interaction, and feedback. We developed SpaceMates, a tangible programming game combining tabletop robots with 3D-printed blocks for children aged 7–10. Children construct 3D structures, plan routes with height variations, and compare intended and executed paths through robot feedback. Based on developmental trajectories of spatial skills in middle childhood and the Spatial Reasoning Instrument (SRI), we designed tasks for ages 7–8 and 9–10. In study with 30 participants, we examined within- and between-condition changes. Unadjusted tests suggested MR and SV gains for ages 7–8 and SO gains for ages 9–10 in SpaceMates, with greater SO gains than Baseline. In Holm-adjusted analyses, only the pre–post SO change among participants aged 9–10 remained statistically significant; after adjustment, no between-condition gain comparison remained statistically significant. Behavioral analyses characterized interaction patterns.
